id: Dream Ending in a Host of Angels Zipping Me into My Grandmother’s Dress

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Once & could-be-future girl, believe we’re not like you. Sure, the pickup was tucked in dusk, shed all carefree w/ its sunburn shimmer. Still nothing new to say about the creek, how reeds get moony, or when we saw pelicans hold hands & gossip. But y’all must wanna get this close to soft, so here goes: spool heels, silver sleeves w/ pink accents, kind to stifle the trailer static, same color Dot says Granny passed in. Past since good & we did keep her pearls for you, kissed the hems holy, darned the moth marks back to true. Goes: none of it imitation. Goes: we are her barefoot bloodline, butter in the salt pan. Trust you’re not from this sweat but still a goodness. You once most only boy in the yard, laugh into your born polish. Step-joy, uncousin: home is a name you bless in silk & cinch. Believe we’re all alive here. Come hum this lace blood-warm. Glisten.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Once, Sure, Still

outputs.L1:
Once and could-be-future girl, believe this: we are not like you. True, the pickup was tucked into dusk, shedding all its carefreeness with that sunburnt shimmer. Still, there is nothing new to say about the creek, about how the reeds turn moony, or about the time we saw pelicans hold hands and gossip.

But y’all must want to get this close to softness, so here goes: spool heels; silver sleeves with pink accents; kindness enough to stifle the trailer static; the same color Dot says Granny passed in. Passed since good, and we did keep her pearls for you, kissed the hems holy, darned the moth marks back to true.

Here it goes: none of it is imitation. Here it goes: we are her barefoot bloodline, butter in the salt pan. Trust that you are not from this sweat, but still a goodness. You, once the most-only boy in the yard, laughing into your born polish. Step-joy, uncousin: home is a name you bless in silk and cinch.

Believe we are all alive here. Come hum this lace, blood-warm. Glisten.
outputs.L2:
Once-girl and maybe-girl-to-come, trust this: we are not the same as you.

Yes, the truck sat hidden in the evening light, stripped of its easy sun-glare shine. There is still nothing original to add about the creek, about the reeds turning lunar, or about the time we watched pelicans clasp together and murmur like neighbors.

But maybe you want to come near something tender, so listen: spool heels, silver sleeves touched with pink, gentle enough to hush the trailer’s crackle, the very shade Dot says Granny wore when she died. She has been gone a long time, and we saved her pearls for you. We kissed the hems as if making them sacred, mended the moth-eaten places until they were whole again.

Here it is: none of this is pretending. Here it is: we come from her bare feet and her blood, soft as butter set in a pan of salt. We know you were not made from this sweat, but you are still a kind of good.

You, who were once almost the only boy in the yard, laughing inside the polish you were born with. Step-joy, not-quite-cousin: home is a word you honor in silk and tightened seams.

Believe this: everyone here is living. Come sing close to this lace, warm as blood.

Shine.
outputs.L3:
The poem is addressed to a “could-be-future girl,” someone who seems to represent another possible version of femininity, identity, or belonging. From the beginning, however, the speaker makes clear that her own community and lived experience are not the same as the addressee’s. She insists on the distinctiveness of her world, suggesting that it cannot be easily copied, claimed, or understood from the outside. The speaker’s voice is protective and self-assured, drawing a boundary around the people, places, and memories that have shaped her.

The setting of the poem is rural, intimate, and deeply sensory. It evokes a landscape of dusk, a creek, reeds, pelicans, and the closeness of trailer life. These details create a world that feels both humble and sacred, marked by ordinary surroundings that carry emotional and cultural significance. The natural imagery blends with domestic imagery, so that the creek, the birds, the fading light, and the trailer become part of the speaker’s sense of home. This environment is not merely background; it is central to the speaker’s identity and to the community she describes.

Clothing and inherited objects also play an important role in the poem. The speaker describes garments, pearls, and repaired fabric as more than material possessions. They are sacred links to Granny and to family memory. The worn or mended quality of these items gives them value rather than diminishing them, because they carry the touch, labor, and survival of previous generations. Through these objects, the speaker honors ancestry and presents family inheritance as something spiritual, intimate, and alive.

A major emphasis of the poem is the authenticity of the speaker’s identity. She rejects the idea that she is imitating anyone or performing a borrowed version of herself. Instead, her identity is rooted in ancestry, hardship, place, and lived experience. The poem suggests that what may appear to outsiders as style, costume, or attitude is actually the result of family history and survival. The speaker’s selfhood is not decorative; it is inherited, earned, and embodied.

Despite the speaker’s firm distinction between her world and the addressee’s, the poem also opens toward welcome. By the end, the speaker invites the “could-be-future girl” into a warm and blessed vision of home, kinship, and shared aliveness. The invitation does not erase difference, but it offers connection. The poem ultimately presents home as a sacred space made of memory, land, family, and care—a place where identity is honored and where others may be welcomed if they approach with respect.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores inheritance, belonging, and gendered kinship through a lush, intimate address that blends rural imagery, family relics, and sensory detail. Its speaker seems to move through memory as though moving through a landscape: fields, houses, heirlooms, and bodies all become part of the same emotional terrain. Rather than treating ancestry as something distant or purely historical, the poem makes it feel immediate and tactile. The past appears in objects that can be held, in names that can be spoken, in gestures passed from one generation to another, and in the natural world that surrounds the family line.

At the center of the poem is a tender meditation on what it means to belong. Belonging is not presented as simple bloodline or fixed origin; instead, it is something made and remade through recognition, care, and blessing. The speaker’s relationship to family history is complicated by questions of gender and identity, but the poem does not frame transformation as a break from ancestry. On the contrary, it suggests that becoming oneself can be a way of returning more deeply to the love that came before.

The poem’s imagery gives this idea emotional force. Rural details evoke continuity, growth, and rootedness, while family relics suggest the weight of memory and tradition. Sensory language—touch, scent, sound, and visual richness—makes inheritance feel embodied rather than abstract. The speaker is not merely thinking about home; they are feeling it through the body, through the land, and through the remembered presence of kin.

Ultimately, the poem finds a generous vision of lineage. It argues that chosen or transformed identity can still be held within ancestral love. Home, then, is not a single place, a stable category, or an unchanged past. It is a living connection: something blessed, carried, revised, and renewed through love.
outputs.L5:
Once, there was a quiet moment when everything seemed uncertain. The path ahead was not clear, and every choice felt heavier than the last. Still, there was a small spark of hope that refused to disappear.

“Are you sure?” someone asked.

No one could be completely sure. Life rarely offers perfect answers. But sometimes, being sure is not about knowing exactly what will happen. It is about trusting yourself enough to take the next step.

Once that step is taken, things begin to change. Fear may still remain, and doubts may still whisper, but courage grows with every move forward. In the end, even the smallest decision can become the beginning of something meaningful.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short prose poem in a Southern Gothic, queer, lyrical voice addressed to a “once & could-be-future girl,” with imagery of trailers, creeks, heirloom clothes, pearls, and inherited femininity.
counterfactuals.output: Once & could-be-future girl, I kept your name in the rusted mouth of the trailer, where kudzu climbed the windows like a widow’s hands. Down by the creek, we washed our knees of red clay and called it baptism, though the water knew better, carrying off our borrowed sins in minnows and oil-slick rainbows. Your mama’s slip hung on the line like a ghost learning weather; my grandmother’s pearls cooled in my palm, each one a tiny moon we were told to swallow. We inherited femininity the way some inherit debt: lace-yellowed, perfumed with mothballs, pinned too tight at the throat. Still, when you looked at me in that heirloom dress, hem muddy, lipstick blooming dark as a bruise, I saw a future rise from the rot—sweet, feral, and forbidden—waiting to be worn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental second-person poem about welcoming a trans girl into a rural Southern family, using lush fragmented language, ampersands, and images like pelicans, dusk, silver sleeves, pink accents, and a grandmother’s pearls.
counterfactuals.output:
You arrive at dusk & the porch  
remembers how to open—  

screen door sighing  
like a hymn half-sung,  
moths stitching the hot air  
with silver sleeves.  

You, girl, with your pink accents—  
ribbon, blush, nail, laugh—  
small flags of yourself  
fluttering in the magnolia dark.  

The family gathers not like judgment  
but like rainwater in a barrel,  
each face tilted toward you,  
each hand learning the shape  
of welcome.  

Out past the pasture, pelicans  
cross the bruised sky  
as if the coast has flown inland  
just to bless you.  

Your grandmother fastens her pearls  
around your throat—  
one moon, then another,  
then another—  
& says nothing at first  
because love is sometimes  
a quiet clasp,  

because blood can be chosen  
again & again  
at the kitchen table,  
over okra, cornbread,  
sweet tea sweating through the glass.  

You stand there shining  
in the rural hush,  
not new, no—  
newly seen.  

& the house, old as red clay,  
old as mule-song,  
leans close  
with every window lit,  

saying:  

come in, daughter,  
come in,  
we saved you a plate,  
we saved you your name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, contemporary prose-poem that sounds like a hybrid of prayer, family gossip, and fashion description; include “Goes:” as a repeated phrase and end with the word “Glisten.”
counterfactuals.output: Blessed be the aunties in their lacquered mules, clicking through the apartment like small verdicts; blessed be the cousin who arrived late in a citron slipdress, saying traffic when everyone knew it was desire; blessed be the grandmother’s rings, swollen on her fingers like tiny planets refusing orbit, and the beige sofa receiving all our secrets without blinking. Goes: the story of who borrowed money and returned it as perfume. Goes: the story of who married for papers, then love, then spite. Goes: the story of the hemline rising with the rent, the neckline plunging with the temperature of the room. Lord, keep us immaculate in bad lighting, keep our silk unwrinkled through grief, keep the group chat merciful and the screenshots buried. My mother, in black organza, says don’t repeat this, then crowns the table with it; my sister powders her throat and forgives no one; the baby sleeps under a constellation of gold bangles and half-prayers. Goes: your father saw her at the clinic. Goes: her bag is real but her laugh is borrowed. Goes: I am not judging, I am only noticing, which is our family’s oldest religion. Outside, the city kneels in chrome and rain, every storefront dressed for resurrection, every window arranging its mannequins like saints with sharper collarbones. We pass the salad, the blame, the lipstick; we pass the dead names under our tongues and call it dinner. O velvet God of elevators and emergency exits, O sequined Mother of second chances, pin us into our better silhouettes, zip us closed before we spill. Let the beloveds who left us be seen in the sheen of a patent boot, in the flash of a cousin’s tooth, in the oil on the soup, in the rumor returning changed but radiant. Let what was hidden come softly, not as punishment but as satin. Let the whole house, overdressed and unforgiven, Glisten.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in an ornate, intimate, Southern vernacular style about ancestry, softness, gender transformation, and home, addressing someone as “step-joy” and “uncousin,” with references to a creek, trailer static, spool heels, and lace.
counterfactuals.output:
Step-joy, come sit where the porchlight hushes itself gold.

I been thinking on blood and not-blood, on the way a family can be a quilt stitched from dresses nobody wears no more, feed-sack cotton and funeral black, lace gone tea-brown at the edges. Some folks say ancestry is a straight-backed thing, all Bible pages and courthouse names, but I know better, uncousin. I know it come up crooked as creek root, singing under mud, carrying bottle glass, crawdad shell, and the soft old prayers of women who learned to braid thunder into supper.

You came home changed, which is to say you came home truer.

Don’t let nobody make a courtroom out your body. Don’t let nobody call your blooming a betrayal. The magnolia don’t apologize for opening, even when the heat lays down heavy as a hand. I seen you in them spool heels, wobbling first like a newborn deer, then walking clean through the trailer static—TV snow hissing in the dark room, aunties pretending not to look, uncles coughing into their coffee. But the walls knew. The linoleum knew. The mirror over the sink, with its little black freckles, knew. It had been waiting on you to arrive.

Softness ain’t weakness, step-joy. Softness is the creek wearing stone down patient. Softness is biscuit dough under floury knuckles. Softness is your grandmama’s slip, lace-hemmed and holy, surviving cedar trunks, floodwater, moth-hunger, and every mouth that said hush. You got that same surviving on you. You carry a lineage not just of names, but of gestures: wrist-turn, hip-sway, chin lifted against weather. Every girl you ever were not allowed to be is walking with you now, barefoot through clover.

And home—Lord, home ain’t always kind. Sometimes home is a screen door that slaps too loud, a hallway full of old rules, a bedroom where you learned to fold yourself small. But sometimes home is what we conjure after. A kettle singing. A borrowed dress. Somebody saying, I see you, sugar, and meaning it down to the marrow. Sometimes home is me calling you uncousin because kinship got more imagination than blood ever did.

Come on back by the creek when the evening turns blue. Wear the lace if you want. Wear the heels. Wear your new name like Sunday perfume. I’ll be there with my feet in the water, listening for the ancestors to murmur through the cane—those that bore us, those that dreamed us, those that had to hide their tenderness in hymnals and hemwork.

They know you.

They been knowing.

They were the first ones to call you beautiful.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal rural elegy for a grandmother’s passed-down dress and pearls, spoken to an outsider or newly beloved family member, using phrases like “barefoot bloodline,” “butter in the salt pan,” and “Come hum this lace blood-warm.”
counterfactuals.output:
Come closer, you newly named kin,  
you stranger with rain still shining in your coat—  
this was her dress, hung in the cedar dark,  
blue as dusk milk, thin as a field’s last breath.

She wore it when the cows came home  
with moonlight tangled in their horns,  
when the well coughed up stars,  
when the road unspooled like a black ribbon  
from the mouth of the pines.

Here are her pearls—  
not jewels, no, not exactly.  
Small moons she worried between finger and thumb,  
a rosary of creek stones,  
eggs of the old white hens,  
teeth of every winter she survived.

She was our barefoot bloodline,  
heel-deep in clover, storm, and sorrow,  
singing to the beans so they would climb,  
pressing her shadow into the porch boards  
until even the house learned to miss her.

Do not be afraid of the stains.  
That one is blackberry, that one is birth,  
that one is butter in the salt pan,  
gold gone strange in the noon heat.  
The darker one—leave it unnamed.  
Every family has a weather  
it folds away.

When she died, the pasture bowed.  
The scarecrow removed his hat.  
All night, the jars in the cellar  
filled themselves with fireflies  
and the mule cried human at the fence.

Now I lay this dress across your arms  
like a field laid under snow.  
Take the pearls; hear them clicking—  
little bones of Sunday, little ghosts of cream.  
Wear them when the kitchen windows bloom with frost,  
when grief comes lowing through the yard.

Come hum this lace blood-warm.  
Let it learn your throat.  
You are no longer outside the door.  
The dead have measured you in lamplight  
and found room.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
